(b)	the criteria to be used to assess the bilingualism of such a person,
(c)	the length of such an inquiry,
(d)	ascertaining whether a business is French Canadian or not.
In addition, we feel that knowledge of the facts, of statistics and of the degree of participation of French Canadians in the affairs of the country is absolutely essential to the Laurendeau-Dunton royal commission if it is to conduct a worthwhile inquiry.
On the other hand, we understand and appreciate that the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) would like to dispose of all the questions on the order paper before the summer recess.

subtopic: GREAT LAKES

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: GREAT LAKES
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DECISION TO ESTABLISH TRUSTEESHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I indicated yesterday that I should like to make a further statement about the report of Mr. Justice Norris on the disruption of shipping. Hon. members will have had the opportunity of reading the report and becoming familiar with its contents since its release just over two weeks ago on July 18. Hon. members will, I think, all agree with me that the commissioner delivered a comprehensive report following one oi tne most intensive inquiries ever made in Canada in a labour relations situation. The report gives an account of violence, corruption, lawlessness, mismanagement, misapplication of union funds and arbitrary control over the livelihood of seamen on the waters of the great lakes and the St. Lawrence seaway.
Both the inquiry itself and the report have clearly stirred public opinion, and from questions asked by hon. members it would appear that they have also been deeply shocked by the sordid and cynical situation which appears to exist in areas of the shipping industry on the joint waters uniting Canada and the United States. A strong desire has been expressed that resolute action be taken to control the situation, to cure it and to prevent it from corrupting other parts of the legitimate union movement.
An interdepartmental committee composed of deputy ministers and other senior officials of the departments most directly concerned was named, as announced earlier, on July 17. This committee has reviewed, under some pressure, the recommendations contained in the report and has made its observations on each of them. Based on these observations, on the endorsation of the major recommendation on the part of four of the five maritime unions directly involved, one of which endorsed the major recommendation only yesterday, and on the widespread public support for effective action to be taken to deal with the


situation revealed by the inquiry, the government has reached a decision that a trusteeship is advisable.
Consultations have been carried on with the Canadian Labour Congress about the course of action which might be followed. Both the government and the Canadian Labour Congress hold firmly to the view that a government sponsored trusteeship should not be introduced as a normal means of dealing with problems arising within or between unions, and that it is justified in this instance only due to the extraordinary circumstances prevailing with respect to Canadian shipping on the great lakes and the St. Lawrence seaway.
In view of the fact that all of its affiliates concerned have accepted the recommendation for a trusteeship, and on the understanding that a trusteeship would be of a temporary duration and that the legislation providing for it would contain other safeguards, including progressive removal of the trusteeship, the Canadian Labour Congress has now assured the government of its co-operation.
A start has been made on the preparation of the necessary legislation. As will be appreciated, this requires much care due to the conctituticncil aspect involved necessity for the legislation to be effective.
We had hoped it would have been possible to bring forward legislation before the recess. The only type of legislation that could have been prepared for immediate parliamentary action, due to the limited time available since the report was issued, would have been general enabling legislation empowering the government to take the necessary action under regulations approved by governor in council.
After careful reflection it has been decided not to propose this course. Instead a decision has been taken to press ahead with the preparation of detailed legislation that is within the power of parliament to enact, and which will be introduced for the immediate attention of the house on our return at the end of September.
The interval will enable us to proceed with our plans, including completion of the necessary work on the legislation. It is our intention to have further discussions with the United States authorities with a view to ensuring the maximum effectiveness of a trusteesship in removing the continuing harassment of Canadian ships on the great lakes. I would like to refer, in this connection, to that portion of the official release issued in May following the meeting of President Kennedy and the Prime Minister of Canada at Hyannis Port on May 11:
"On the great waters that separate and unite the two countries-the St. Lawrence river and the great lakes-it is essential that those who own

and sail the ships should be free to go about their lawful business without impediment or harassment."
As hon. members know, this harassment has continued. There have been several further acts of violence, illegal picketing, and one Canadian vessel has been refused the right of all shipping and loading facilities at the port of Chicago for over 100 days, despite the fact that court injunctions against such secondary picketing have been obtained.
It is to be sincerely hoped that the decision to establish a trusteeship will lead to a full resolution of the serious problems that have arisen in both Canada and the United States over the past three shipping seasons.
Trusteeship, which is a device used by the unions themselves to control and rehabilitate delinquent local unions, is a distasteful remedy to deal with a repugnant situation. Fortunately nearly everyone has realized that action along these lines is a necessity and has endorsed the commissioner's recommendation in this respect. While the government has every expectation of co-operation on the part of all responsible Canadian and United States union members and leaders and of all companies directly concerned, I do want to make it clear that should matters deteriorate on the great lakes or elsewhere, and it becomes necessary, parliament will be called back into session earlier than has been announced to deal with this matter.
In any event, sustained efforts will be maintained during our recess to see that cooperation with the United States authorities is developed to the fullest possible extent so that it will serve to supplement action taken by parliament. The interval may in fact prove useful not only to develop these supplementary lines of action but also to permit substitute action being taken should this prove to be equally effective in accomplishing the objectives of the legislation now being prepared.
I should add, Mr. Speaker, before concluding that the two special counsel, Mr. Robinette of Toronto and Mr. Martineau of Montreal, have already commenced their examination of the report of the inquiry commission and the accompanying exhibits and documents, and will be in a position to advise the government in due course with respect to prosecutions.

subtopic: GREAT LAKES
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DECISION TO ESTABLISH TRUSTEESHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the house welcome the announcement that has been made by the Minister of Labour that the government has decided to put into effect by legislation the most important of the recommendations made
Establishment of Shipping Trusteeship by Mr. Justice Norris; that is, the recommendation to set up a trusteeship. I wish to say a few more words about that later.
First may I say that as minister of labour at the time this commission was set up I found it necessary, because of conditions existing on the great lakes, to take this action. We were very fortunate indeed to obtain the services of Mr. Justice Norris of British Columbia as the commissioner. Mr. Justice Norris did a wonderful piece of work in getting all the evidence after well over 100 meetings during the course of his investigation and in writing, as the Minister of Labour has stated, a very comprehensive report dealing, I might say, with a very serious situation which faced operations on the great lakes.
The interdepartmental committee which has been working since July 17 has certainly done a very effective job in its recommendations to the government, and it is well that the government has heeded the advice of Mr. Justice Norris and the interdepartmental committee in deciding to set up a trusteeship. I think this is advisable. I want to congratulate the Canadian Labour Congress and the other unions affiliated with them for their attitude in agreeing to operate under government trusteeship. Mind you, Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of Labour has said, it is distasteful to organized labour and very repugnant to them to be placed under trusteeship. Nevertheless I think the situation warrants this being done, but it should be on a very temporary basis. In other words the members of the trusteeship should work toward achieving a peaceful solution to the problem on the great lakes in as short a space of time as possible. Certainly it should not be a precedent for any case in the future unless the situation warrants it, as it did on the great lakes. I think it is very important that its duration be not too long, yet it should be sufficient to carry out the recommendations which have been made by Mr. Justice Norris.
I think another important aspect is the harassment of Canadian ships in United States ports. Since the government is willing to take decisive action through legislation, the United States government should be asked to take some more definite action in co-operation with the Canadian government in order to see that Canadian ships are able to put into United States ports and be loaded and unloaded without undue delay, which has not been the case with Canadian ships up to now, and as has not been the case with the Canadian ship now tied up in the port of Chicago.
The Minister of Labour mentioned that if the situation demands, or if there is any disruption on the great lakes between now and

Establishment of Shipping Trusteeship the time the legislation is introduced, parliament may be recalled. I hope the government, and particularly the Minister of Labour and his department, will keep a very sharp lookout for such an eventuality and that they will do everything in their power to bring about a settlement; and I hope there will be no disruption of shipping on the great lakes between now and the time the legislation is enacted.

We commend the four of five unions which have agreed to go into trusteeship in recognition of this problem. We hope the Minister of Justice will not overlook the responsibility that we feel his department has in perusing and following up the subject matter of the report regarding possible prosecutions which should be muds' and. f'u'^prmnrp wp hops the Department of Justice will not overlook the alleged collusion between some shipping companies and the labour unions.
We too agree that this kind of action should not be considered as a precedent for curing labour problems, although we think it is necessary in this most extreme case. I listened carefully, but I do not think the Minister of Labour mentioned any effective date for the establishment of this trusteeship. We also recognize the international problems which are involved, and we appreciate the difficulties here because of the tie between the union in Canada and the union in the United States. We hope that the government, as the hon. member for Ontario suggested, will take further steps to persuade the United States government to take action which will prevent this harassment of Canadian ships in United States ports.

subtopic: GREAT LAKES
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DECISION TO ESTABLISH TRUSTEESHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the Minister of Labour is to be commended for the statement he has just made regarding the action which the government proposes to take arising out of the report of the Norris commission. I think he is particularly to be commended for having


consulted the Canadian Labour Congress, representing, as it does, the great bulk of the labour movement in this country; because the Canadian Labour Congress has been fully justified by the Norris report both in asking for the investigation in the first place and in the material which it submitted to the Norris commission in its brief presented last March. The fact that the minister has consulted with them and secured their co-operation will make it much easier to deal with this difficult situation.
This abnormal and disgraceful situation arose out of three factors. It arose out of a racketeering union, the seafarers international union, with the collusion of certain steamship companies, in particular the Canada Steamship Lines, which co-operated with Mr. Banks in breaking the laws of Canada. The third factor was the laxity of government administration. It was known the law was being broken, but no action was taken in this regard.
The proposal of Mr. Justice Norris for a trusteeship is something we normally would not support. Democratically elected, clean unions ought not to be put under government trusteeship. But the seafarers international union is not a democratic, clean uuioii. The evidence which was presented by the Canadian Labour Congress and which is fully corroborated in the report of Mr. Justice Norris proves that the S.I.U. is a cancerous growth on labour unions and on the body politic. Therefore I think the government has no choice but to place this union under a trusteeship.	_
Fortunately the other unions, which were given a clean bill of health by Mr. Justice Norris, have indicated their willingness voluntarily to come under this trusteeship as the quickest means of dealing with an unfortunate situation, and I think they are to be congratulated on this attitude. However, I would say the government is to be commended on declining to proceed with general legislation. I do not think we could support general legislation giving the government power to bring any union under trusteeship. I think the government is wise to wait until it can bring down specific legislation dealing with a union which has proved to be racketeers and dealing with unions which are willing to come within the scope of this trusteeship.
I hope the government will also give consideration to the position of the companies which have compounded this felony, particularly the Canada Steamship Lines, for the part they have played in this unfortunate and disgraceful situation. I would also hope the government could make some progress toward getting the co-operation of the government of

the United States in dealing with the position of Canadian ships which are in United States ports. There is a ship called the Red Wing at the ore dock in Marquette, Michigan. I am told the railway to the dock has been dynamited in recent days. Another ship was fired upon when it approached port facilities. This is a situation which cannot be allowed to continue, and I hope the government will be able to bring pressure to bear on the government of the United States to see that Canadian ships and seamen are protected.
One other point should be kept in mind. What is to happen in the meantime to the union funds of the seafarers' international union? I am told Mr. Banks has already placed a levy of $50 each on all his members in order that he may be in a position to fight any action which might be taken arising out of the Norris report. These funds may be badly misused and mishandled prior to any legislative action being taken. I therefore say to the minister and to the government that if they get this legislation ready soon and it looks as though union funds are being misused, and the situation is becoming more serious, they should have no hesitation about calling parliament back into session for two or three days in order to protect the members of the unions and to protect the public interest of the people of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Guy Favreau (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF ESKIMO AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that I was informed this morning of the statement made by that provincial official, Mr. Gourdeau, and that I was amazed that in the absence of the minister, Mr. Levesque, that civil servant should take the liberty to criticize, on behalf of the provincial government, the attitude of two federal ministers.
In regard to the statement that the federal government unduly and unfairly delayed the negotiations concerning the transfer of the Eskimo affairs administration, I think it would be interesting for all the members of this house to know that it concerns both the present and the previous governments and that they both are in the same situation.
In 1935, it was the province of Quebec itself which asked the Supreme Court of Canada to state that the responsibilities for Eskimo affairs should rest, not with the province of Quebec, but exclusively with the federal government. The decision was made in 1939, so that was 24 years ago. Now, suddenly, it was decided this year that the province should take over Eskimo affairs.
We could have quite a discussion on the matter and I respect everyone's opinion, but I must say that before the federal government, or rather before the minister of northern affairs and myself should recommend to the government to abdicate its responsibilities in matters concerning the Eskimos 24 years after the decision made by the supreme court and during which period we assumed responsibility in the matter, we must be entirely satisfied that it would be in the interest of the Eskimos and that all facilities would be made available to them. Then, and only then will the recommendation be made.
It should be noted that at a time when parliament was extremely busy, a meeting was held on June 26; discussions were held under friendly conditions, and we offered to meet the minister of natural resources during our holidays; therefore, it is unfair for a provincial official to accuse us, on behalf of his government, of delaying the negotiations. After all, a month's delay compared to 24 years is very little.

Inquiries of the Ministry
So, it is no exaggeration to state here that the minister of northern affairs and myself are still at the disposal of the provincial minister, but not necessarily at the disposal of Mr. Gourdeau, in order to set the date for a meeting as soon as possible.
I may add that I did not know Mr. Rene Levesque had delegated his powers to Mr. Gourdeau and that he had not informed me that a summit conference was to be held between two federal ministers and a provincial official.

speechtext:
This clause has the effect of repealing the National Productivity Council Act, and the reason we asked that clause 11 stand was because it was related and conveys to the economic council the duties of the national productivity council. Subclause 2 of clause 11 provides that projects initiated under subclause 1 will revert to government departments as soon as this can be done. This means the elimination and burial of the national productivity council and its work, first by disbanding it and second by transferring its duties to this new council, with provision for progressive reversion of those duties to various departments of government. But the theme and principle of the productivity council was that it should deal with those problems-and there are a great many of them-which require the co-operation of management and labour; that it should deal with them on the basis of mutual co-operation.
I was very interested indeed in and impressed by the words uttered yesterday in this repect by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs who, if I understood him correctly, looked upon the work of the national productivity council with great favour. He felt, as I am sure do many hon. members, especially the hon. member for Fraser Valley, that the national productivity council certainly made great strides in the field of management and labour cooperation and broke new ground in this area, establishing a principle that has taken hold.
Once these projects revert to a government department, that principle of dual labour-management approach is completely abrogated in favour of a purely departmental approach. This, to my mind, involves such matters as productivity, labour-management relations, automation, training and retraining of workers; in short, a whole area of the industrial complex which can best be served, I submit, by a joint labour-management approach, with government being the recipient of their joint recommendations. Just a few moments

Economic Council of Canada ago an amendment was moved-perhaps I should not refer to that amendment because it was passed-and certain things will only be made public as certain people see fit to make them public. Recommendations are not to be made available to everyone concerned, neither labour nor management. The effect of this clause and the clause that has been stood, No. 11, is to remove these matters from the purview of labour and management in this country and transfer them to the government. I think this is a step backward. The principle we put into effect has taken great strides in the past few years since the inception of the national productivity council and has brought about greater labour-management co-operation in a field in which both these factors are very vitally interested.
Clause 22 removes from existence the only government body which labour and management can meet to deal with problems that are peculiar to labour and management but which nevertheless make their effects felt throughout our whole economy. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that no substitute body should be set up because the duties would be taken over in such a way as to provide for their eventual parcelling out among government departments. I look at this as a process of assassination by attrition. The Liberal party when in opposition did not believe in the productivity council from its inception, and throughout its existence there was nothing but bitter and harsh criticism of the council from members of that party. But I submit it was only a political attack. Although the president of the Canadian Labour Congress, after accepting a position on this council, objected to the make-up of the council because he felt there was not sufficient representation on it from industrial unions, he at no time criticized the principle of labour-management co-operation embodied in the work of the council. Since the inception of the council and the work they have carried out in the labour-management field I am glad to note that he has become one of the greatest supporters of the labour-management principle and is continually advocating more and more of this sort of thing in order to help resolve the difficulties which present themselves in our economy. This bill, and particularly this clause, destroys that whole principle.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that clause 22 should be deleted from the bill before us, which would have the effect of continuing the productivity council and would eliminate the necessity for the inclusion of clause 11, which should also be deleted. I therefore move:
That clause 11 and clause 22 of Bill No. C-72 be deleted.

I should like to pay a compliment to the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk) for his activity in this connection last year and again on this occasion, and to two former members of the house who are no longer with us, Mr. Robert McCleave of Halifax and Mr. Doug Morton of Toronto, who worked many long hours attempting to arrive at a solution to this very vexing problem.
The problem has been recognized by all members of the house for many years, and a very great effort was made, involving the expenditure of many hours of time in attempting to reach a solution to the problem, one which has escaped solution for a very long period of Canada's history. There were several occasions on which two or three of us representing the various parties in the house conferred with Mr. Speaker Michener about the problem. Some members of the house conferred with members of the other place. A great deal of work was done in that way in order to achieve success.
Two years ago a bill almost identical to this one was passed by this chamber with the co-operation of all hon. members but it failed to receive approval in the other place. Now we have finally arrived at the stage where agreement has been reached. Certain additions have been made in this bill which have provided for valid objections raised on other occasions. I hope there will be general agreement to the passing of the bill and thus removing a very contentious problem from this chamber.
At the same time we will have to push into the background and forget some of the controversy we have had in this chamber with regard to methods that were used to promote the idea of a change in procedure with respect to divorce. The great thing today is that we now have an achievement which I think will be creditable to parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
In speaking to the resolution in the house on June 11 and in reply to the debate on the resolution on June 17, I set
Municipal Development and Loan Board forth the purposes of the municipal development and loan act and explained the manner in which it would contribute to employment.
While the financial assistance given in this legislation will help municipalities to build capital works, it must be remembered that the primary purpose is to give employment. This we hope to accomplish by increasing the level of municipal capital expenditure over the next two or three years, that is, up to March 31, 1966 which is the terminal date specified in the bill.
The speeding up of municipal capital expenditure is to be accomplished by making loans available to municipalities on favourable terms. A municipal loan fund of $400 million will be established for this purpose. The money will be available to the municipalities for financing additional capital projects and the interest rate will be the government's own long term rate plus not more than one quarter of 1 per cent administrative overhead charges. To provide an added incentive for a rapid increase in municipal capital spending, the government will forgive one quarter of the loan made with respect to the increased capital spending before March 31, 1966. This, of course, is the equivalent of a major reduction in the rate of interest on the full amount of the loan.
I should like to repeat that. There are two ways of providing money for this particular purpose on a basis that will be attractive to the municipalities. One would be at a reduced interest rate. The other is the one proposed in this bill which provides for a substantial forgiveness feature of part of the capital. They both have the same effect.
This then is the broad outline of the program: A fund of $400 million available to finance additional municipal capital expenditures up to March 31, 1966, an interest rate on loans equal to the federal long term rate plus a moderate overhead charge, and a 25 per cent forgiveness of the amount of the loan made with respect to work completed up to March 31, 1966.
The whole plan is designed to make a substantial contribution to employment in the coming winter and over the next two or three years. The main purpose of the plan, to increase employment by the above means, has been endorsed by the provinces, and I might say it has been endorsed by all of the provinces. This is demonstrated by the joint communique issued at the conclusion of the meeting on July 26 and 27 with the provinces, which began as follows:
The meeting of federal and provincial governments has concluded with full agreement on the proposal of the federal government to promote employment by financial assistance, with provincial approval and co-operation, to municipal capital works.
2908	HOUSE OF
Municipal Development and Loan Board
As a result of the meeting with the provinces last week end I will propose certain changes in the legislation which have to do with the method of administration and with the breadth of the program. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has already referred to the excellent results of the conference. Speaking in the house on July 29 he referred to the very satisfactory agreement reached between the federal government and the provinces. He pointed out that the conference with the provinces had accomplished all that it could of itself accomplish. It produced a very satisfactory understanding with the provincial governments about the recommendations the federal government would make to parliament concerning the municipal development and loan bill.
The modifications in which the provinces were particularly interested were of two kinds, and the proposals that we will make to parliament in this connection are summarized in the communique to which I have already referred. The first point has to do with the scope of the program and I should like to quote the communique on this point as follows:
The federal government indicated to the provinces that it will propose, in the legislation to be discussed in parliament next week, features which will enable the measure to be applied in forms adapted to different conditions in the various provinces. The federal government will propose that the range of municipal works covered in the program will be broadened so as to include in any province all those municipal works which the province and the federal government believe to be productive of increased employment.
It was clear from our discussions with the provincial representatives that they felt that broadening the range of programs to which the municipal development and loan bill would apply would make possible a greater contribution to employment and would make for a fairer division of the assistance as between municipalities. Since the government is concerned with achieving the full effect from an employment standpoint and since we are also concerned that the program should be a fair and equitable one from the standpoint of the provinces and the municipalities, we will be proposing an amendment to broaden the list of municipal projects which will be eligible for assistance, provided, of course, that they are additional municipal capital works which will provide additional employment over what we would have had without this plan.
The second modification with respect to administration was also outlined in the communique and I should like to quote the pertinent paragraph:
In response to suggestions from a majority of the provinces-


And, I might say, concurred in by all the provinces.
-the federal government will also propose that, if a province so wishes, it will be able to make with the proposed municipal development and loan board an agreement whereby the province is responsible for granting and administering the loans to municipalities, subject to such safeguards as are necessary to enable the board to report to parliament that expenditures have been properly made according to the purposes of the legislation.
This will give the provinces the broadest possible participation in the administration of the program consistent with the responsibility which the federal board must have to parliament.
The changes with respect to the scope of the program, that is, with respect to the types of municipal projects which will be eligible under the program, and the change with respect to the administrative arrangements by which the provinces can enter into an agreement to administer the loan assistance themselves, have the enthusiastic support of the provinces. In addition, we shall be proposing a change that will ensure that a disproportionate share of the $400 million loan fund will not go to some provinces because tbey are in a nosition to rapidly with certain projects. We will meet this point by proposing an allocation of the fund in proportion to the population of each of the provinces. I might say that this was also enthusiastically endorsed by the provinces last week end.

All the provincial premiers gave approval. Why would they not? They got everything they wanted. They got $400 million. They got the forgiveness provision. The scheme now presented bears little or no relationship to the original. In that connection I refer to the Prime Minister's glowing words to the Federation of Mayors and Municipalities on May 29. This plan bears little or no relationship to anything proposed by the Liberals in the election. It now resembles tbs wintsr works program of the former government. The federal government produced its plan and then the provinces rebelled against it. I use that word in the sense that they remonstrated with fervour, and the government, following a pattern familiar in this session of parliament, retreated. It was not because this plan had not been thought of previously. Members of the government had been talking about it for the last several years and had it in mind ever since "Troubled Canada" was produced. I shall later refer to the plan put forward by the Minister of Finance in that famous work, because it bears very little resemblance to the present one.

Municipal works belong to that sector, since they are useful to the community, and also provincial and federal works, for the same reason.
Well, as I said, those works are useful to the community; they make a country richer and bring prosperity.
Why could we not use also a public agency to create the public capital that would be used to pay the cost of that progress which helps the community? By doing so, we would not be compelled, as we are today, to borrow and pay interest and to repay to private enterprise, money which we are using to develop public capital in this country and stimulate progress in the public sector.


Mr. Speaker, this is an important amendment and we are going to move it. Whenever we, of the Social Credit party, were speaking of municipal loans, we always added the words "through the Bank of Canada" and "at the expense of the administration". The Bank of Canada is an organization subject to government, to the crown, or rather to parliament. It is an organization that has been created by parliament, of which we are members.
The Bank of Canada exists today because members elected by the people in a democratic way stood up one day in this house and voted for the establishment of the organization which we call "The Bank of Canada".
The Bank of Canada comes under parliament since it was established by parliament. It belongs to the Canadian people and we are responsible for it because it was set up and it operates by virtue of a federal statute.
Therefore, if we carry the responsibility for the bank, let us make sure that it fulfils the purpose for which it was established, that is to help in the development and progress of our country in the field of public facilities.
Mr. Speaker. I submit that if we were to take the money from the Bank of Canada instead of borrowing it from private enterprise and chartered banks and put it in the consolidated revenue fund, there would not be one penny more in circulation in Canada and there would be no danger of inflation.
That would not cause inflation. The Minister of Finance knows full well what inflation is, since he gave us a sample when he established the tax on building materials which has caused the price of buildings to go up and depreciated our dollar. That is inflation!
The Minister of Finance knows what inflation is, Mr. Speaker, because he takes steps which will cause inflation.
I would not look kindly upon any member opposite who would claim that inflation is caused by Social Crediters because they themselves are the ones responsible for it.
Inflation is something which is blown up. It is inflated money, like a blown-up balloon. The government's 11 per cent tax is such a balloon. In other words, before long our dollar will be worth nothing.
That is why we call on the government to secure its money from the very source of money, the Bank of Canada. That will not create inflation because there is inflation only

when there is too much money in circulation for the quantity of products available.
Now, the Bank of Canada would issue $400 million of credit, but only at the same rate as municipal development.
The Minister of Finance is an accountant, Mr. Speaker, and when he first came to the house, he was known to be the best accountant in Canada. He must know then that in accounting there is a column for assets and another one for liabilities. The entries in those two columns must balance, and then everything is fine.
I am not quite as good an accountant as the Minister of Finance, but I was able to learn that much in the few classes in accounting that I attended. If the Bank of Canada were asked to put credit in circulation at the same rate, not more rapidly or more slowly, but at exactly the same rate as the development of our municipalities, results would be much more satisfactory. For example, when a muncipality builds a $5 million sewer, $5 million are added to Canada's assets. Then, unavoidably the Minister of Finance will add $5 million in the other column. This means that if the Bank of Canada does such a thing, there is no inflation, since the credit is proportional to the product.
If on the other hand, $7 or $8 million were put in circulation, while development projects in our country would only amount to $5 million, we would unavoidably put too much money in circulation and thus create inflation. Then would appear a few individuals to do as the public relations officers of the Liberal party did at the last election and say that money would become valueless.
Well no, that is not true if, as we increase the wealth of this country by building roads, hospitals, bridges, sewers, water systems, we create the required credit at the same rate, neither more nor less, but only what is needed to pay for the country's development. Then, you do not create inflation.
Mr. Speaker, the money used to pay for all that is but a sign which represents all those developments, which are the things signified.
Money is a sign, an index like the quicksilver found in a thermometer. The mercury rises or falls as the temperature goes up or down. A week ago, in Ottawa, it was very hot; so, up went the mercury. Now that it is not quite so hot, the mercury is going down. As the temperature goes, so goes the mercury.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be brief. There are three points I would like to make on this proposed legislation. The first concerns the approach of the government to the whole problem of federal municipal assistance, the second deals with the philosophy of federal assistance to municipalities, and the third is with regard to the scope of the proposed measure.
In dealing with the first, the question of the government's approach, as soon as I received a copy of Bill C-76 I immediately sent copies to all the municipalities in my constituency and to certain key officials in the department of municipal affairs of British Columbia. Then I paid a visit to my area early in July and contacted these same people. I was amazed to find that not only were the senior officials of the department not consulted but by that time, which was about July 5, they had not received copies of the bill, and I found, certainly with regard to preparation of the bill, that these people had not been consulted.
I am sure if they had been consulted-and this would apply to every province of Canada -what would have come out of the mill would have been completely different from this bill I have in my hand and, as I surmise the new bill will be, when it is amended in committee. For example, I understand from the general comments made by the minister that the provinces will be given an almost completely free hand in how the money is to be used. However, does the minister realize that if it is permitted for municipalities to use it for school construction, this would not apply in British Columbia because in that province municipalities do not spend money on the provision of schools? In some provinces municipalities are able to borrow money from the federal government to finance school construction, whereas in British Columbia they would not be able to do this.
I would submit that even with the forced, rushed conference they had last Friday and Saturday, the results that came out of that did not represent what might have been achieved if there had been formal consultation with the provinces, and through the provinces with the municipalities. If that had taken place the program would have been completely different.
My second point concerns the philosophy of federal assistance to municipalities. When he introduced the resolution, and subsequently, the minister said that the prime and only purpose of this legislation is to promote employment. That is a commendable objective but it does not go far enough. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING SURCHARGE ON IMPORTS ORDER
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-88, respecting an order of His Excellency the Governor General in Council entitled the surcharge on imports order, and to restore certain rates of customs duties and tariff benefits expressed to be withdrawn thereby.


He said: Mr. Speaker, on June 24, 1962 the governor in council passed the surcharge on imports order under the authority of the Customs Tariff and the Financial Administration Act and made an amendment to the import control list under the Export and Import Permits Act. The first order resulted in increased tariffs on certain goods and the second reduced the value of goods that might be brought back by travelling Canadians free of duty.
Section 4 of the Customs Tariff, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, chapter 60, empowers the governor in council by order to withdraw rates of customs duties more favourable than the general tariff and to withdraw the benefit of any tariff more favourable than the general tariff. These powers are unrestricted. There is nothing in the act describing any special circumstances or conditions under which they might be exercised.
Section 22 of the Financial Administration Act, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, chapter 116, empowers the governor in council, on the recommendation of the treasury board, to remit any tax, fee or penalty whenever he considers it in the public interest. The section defines a tax as including any tax, impost, duty or toll and provides, inter alia, that a remission may be total or partial and may be granted in any particular case or class of cases and before the liability therefor arises.
There has been some doubt about the validity of the order passed under this item and, as the house knows, there are cases now before the courts. I should have added that there is doubt as to the validity of the order because in the opinion of justice it should have been approved by parliament. The object of this bill is to validate in parliament what was done at the time.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING SURCHARGE ON IMPORTS ORDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we can make most of the comments we wish to make on this bill when we get into committee, but before it is given second reading there are one or two things that I think should be said. The concluding words of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) are most interesting. If I heard him correctly he said that it is the opinion of justice-I presume he means the Department of Justice-that the order in council of June 24 of last year should have had the approval of parliament. Yet during the last session of parliament, the only session of the twenty fifth parliament, we were told several times that it was the opinion of justice, the same Department of Justice, that no such parliamentary approval was necessary.

I hesitate for a moment in case I have misquoted the present Minister of Justice, but if I have quoted him correctly this is a pretty serious situation. We are in effect being told that the Department of Justice gives one piece of advice one year and another piece of advice the next year. I happen to agree with the advice that is now being given, and if parliament accepts the necessity of passing this bill to validate this legislation it will mean that parliament is concurring in the view that the order in council of June 24, 1962, certainly lacked validity.
I feel in this session, as I felt in the last session, that it was a very serious departure from parliamentary practice and parliamentary tradition when the surcharge order in council of June 24, 1962 was passed, and the seriousness of what was done was compounded when the government of that day refused to bring the matter before parliament and refused even to refer the matter to the Supreme Court of Canada as we requested at that time. It makes the whole business very messy, and this sort of nibbling away at the practices of parliament is not good for democracy.
The Minister of Justice has referred to the contention that was implied in the passing of the surcharge order in council, namely, that the government of that day had the right under one statute to raise customs duties and then the right under another statute to reduce those same duties to the particular levels that that government wanted. We contended in the last session of parliament that in effect what the government of that day had done was to impose taxation without parliamentary approval, and if there is one thing that is most basic to the relationship between parliament and the executive and is a basic relationship of long standing it is that taxation cannot be imposed without parliamentary approval.
The Minister of Justice referred to the section of the Financial Administration Act under which the order in council of June 24, 1962, purported to reduce those taxes which in the first place had been raised. We went over all this many times last year. It is clearly a section that provides for remission in kinds of circumstances that are not covered by the order in council in question. We pointed out last year that there is one subsection in section 22 of the Financial Administration Act that requires publication in the public accounts of all remissions over $1,000 granted under that section. When we asked the minister of national revenue in the last session if a report could be brought down showing these remissions, we were told that it would cost so many thousands of
Surcharge on Imports Order dollars to have this done because records were not being kept in that way. I am satisfied that any competent lawyer studying this matter and finding that subsection in section 22 of the Financial Administration Act, would realize right away that the order in council falls to the ground.
We are being called upon to deal with this matter in another way which I think I have to characterize with the same word I used a moment ago, namely that it is messy. There is a clear rule in our books that we are not supposed to deal with matters that are sub judice. This matter is before the courts. It has been taken to the Exchequer Court of Canada.
I remember very well that at one time the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked the government of that day, which was headed by Mr. St. Laurent, to refer to the Supreme Court of Canada a matter that was being discussed here in parliament. Mr. Ilsley was minister of justice and he got into the argument. He established the point very clearly that we could not be dealing with the matter in two courts of the land, namely parliament and a federal court, at the same time. We are doing that. This question of the validity of the surcharge order in council of June 24, 1962, is before the exchequer court. Whether that court is sitting today or tonight does not matter. The fact is it is before the court and we are dealing with it here. We are, I say, violating one of the basic rules of parliament.
Yet, we seem to have no alternative because of the mess into which we have been put. We often hear it said that the courts are the guardians of our liberties, the guardians of law, the guardians of justice and so on. Here is something that has been referred to the courts; at least it has been taken to the court by parties that have been affected by it. If this legislation were not before us, we might get a decision from the exchequer court as to whether or not the surcharge order in council was legal, whether or not it was valid. I assume if we pass this measure the exchequer court might as well drop the case, and probably will, because there will be no point to proceeding with it. In this case the very serious issue of whether or not this surcharge order in council under which millions of dollars were collected, was valid will never be determined by the court. We will prevent that determination by taking the action we are taking now.
I recognize, as the Minister of Finance said when he gave notice some weeks ago that this measure was going to be brought before us, that we will be in a very awkward position if we do not pass this legislation. If the
2934	HOUSE OF
Surcharge on Imports Order courts were to rule that the order in council was invalid, then the government would have to repay this money to the companies that had filed their cases. However, the ultimate consumers who really paid the extra duty would never have a chance to get their money back. So, Mr. Speaker, as I say, the matter is a mess all around. It is the kind of thing that parliamentary and legislative bodies get into when they avoid following the rules, traditions and practices of parliament of very long standing. I am sure that despite the things that were said, despite the feelings we had about this matter in the last parliament, if the government of that day had brought the matter to parliament and let us decide upon it, we would have shown mercy and forgiveness towards the government for what it had done on June 24.
I know that when I heard the former prime minister announce on the night of June 24, 1962, that this was being done, I took it for granted the order was going to come before parliament. I thought we would have a chance to vote on it. I thought, although it was the sort of thing I was opposed to, we might have to vote for it. We were refused time and time again. T. for one from mv seat over there where my friend from Brantford is now sitting, asked the former prime minister to refer the matter to the courts to clear up this uncertainty. He said, there is no uncertainty; it will not be referred to the courts. The fact that there is uncertainty is now established by the fact the matter has been taken to the courts, and by the fact we are having to deal with it in this legislation that is now before us.
I say, Mr. Speaker, we cannot be too careful in the parliament of Canada about these basic rules. Frankly, what the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) said tonight in the course of his brief remarks puts this thing into an awkward position. We were told in the last session by the former minister of justice that the deputy attorney general and the Department of Justice had said that the surcharge order in council was in order. We were led to believe there was an opinion, but we could not get it. We are told in this session that there is no written opinion. We are told tonight by the present Minister of Justice that the Department of Justice now says there should have been parliamentary approval of that legislation. One of my colleagues behind me is asking whether the present Minister of Justice has a written opinion. I can get many written opinions to the effect that this surcharge order in council was invalid.
I think we are caught. There is nothing we can do about it. I believe we should at least realize the seriousness of the point. 

Parliament as a whole, not just the government, should go through what my friend from Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) referred to a moment ago as a period of repentance. We should be in sack cloth and ashes over what was done to the traditions of parliament.
When we get into committee of the whole on the bill I wish to indicate that I shall seek to move an amendment to clause 3 of the bill because this bill does more than the title implies. The title implies that the bill simply validates the order in council of last June 24 and restores certain rates and duties. Then, there is a clause in the bill which amends the Customs Tariff Act. I draw attention to the fact that there is no reference to that in the title of the bill. That is not quite regular. If we are talking about keeping to the rules, let us keep to the rules even if we are trying to patch up a rule that was broken. I suggest that there should be an amendment to the title to include in it the fact that this bill is also proposing an amendment to the Customs Tariff. What bothers me, and I will deal with it more specifically when we get to clause 3 in committee of the whole, is that clause 3, as it is worded, suggests that, an order of the kind that we had on June 24 ought to be brought before parliament before six months. However, there is an implication in that clause that that kind of order in council, the same kind we had last year, would be valid for at least six months.
I do not believe this was a proper course of action last June 24. I do not believe it would be a proper course of action again to pass an order in council based partly on the Customs Tariff Act, by which duties are raised, and based partly on section 22 of the Financial Administration Act by which duties are lowered. However, the wording of clause 3 of this bill is such as to indicate that for six months such an order in council is valid. This whole thing we have been through points up the tremendous need for any government that is in power, whatever party it is, to remember that it is responsible to parliament, and that it does not have the right to do by order in council anything that is not clearly provided for in some statute of this parliament. It was not provided in the statutes of parliament on June 24 last year for the government of that day to do what it did. The fact that the matter has now been taken to the courts makes that clear, and also the fact that this government realizes it has to validate the legislation in case the court declares the order in council invalid.
I hope, as a result of this experience, we will plug that loophole. In fact, when we get to the committee of the whole the amendment I will propose will plug that loophole and

then I hope we will realize this kind of thing must not be repeated if we are to maintain parliamentary democracy in its proper level.
People generally were amazed at a thing like this when it happened last year, and it was a pretty trying experience in the house that we could not get the opinion of justice, the reasons or justification for the order in council, and could not get the matter referred to the supreme court. We were just told that it was proper, that there was no uncertainty, and all that sort of thing. This, incidentally, is something that seems to get into governments, that a government in power can do whatever it feels it has to do or wants to do. That is not true in our parliamentary democracy. The government and the executive can do only those things parliament gives them authority to do. That is a lesson about which we in the parliament of Canada must ever remind ourselves, and it is a lesseon that we simply must keep.

speechtext:
First of all, I should like to say that this has been a red letter day in the history of parliament, and I want to say that rarely have I seen greater co-operation on all sides of the house.
